title: Basic Network Security Concepts

header.html: 4.1 Explain the importance of basic network security concepts: logical security (encryption in transit and at rest, certificates and PKI, self-signed certificates, identity and access management with MFA, SSO, RADIUS, LDAP, SAML, TACACS+, time-based authentication, authorization with least privilege and role-based access control, geofencing); physical security (cameras, locks); deception technologies (honeypot, honeynet); security terminology (risk, vulnerability, exploit, threat, CIA triad); audits and regulatory compliance (data locality, PCI DSS, GDPR); network segmentation enforcement (IoT and IIoT, SCADA, ICS, OT, guest, BYOD)
the official CompTIA Network+ N10-009 exam objectives, version 4.0

html:
1Terminology and the CIA triad

Term Meaning
Confidentiality Only authorized people can read the data (encryption, access control)
Integrity Data is not altered without detection (hashing, signatures)
Availability Systems and data are usable when needed (redundancy, DDoS defense)
Threat Something that can cause harm (an attacker, a flood)
Vulnerability A weakness (unpatched software, default password)
Exploit The method or code that uses a vulnerability
Risk The likelihood and impact of a threat using a vulnerability

2Logical security

Topic Meaning
Encryption Data in transit (TLS, IPsec, SSH, VPN) and data at rest (disk, database encryption)
Certificates and PKI A public key infrastructure issues certificates signed by a certificate authority to prove identity and enable encryption; self-signed certificates are not trusted by default (testing, internal use)
MFA Two or more factors: something you know, have, are
SSO One sign-in for many applications
RADIUS Centralized authentication for network access (Wi-Fi, VPN, 802.1X); UDP, encrypts only the password
TACACS+ Centralized authentication and authorization for device administration; TCP, encrypts the whole payload; separates authentication, authorization and accounting
LDAP Directory access (389; LDAPS 636)
SAML XML-based federation for web SSO between an identity provider and a service
Time-based authentication Access is allowed only at certain times, or time-based one-time passwords
Authorization What an authenticated user may do: least privilege, role-based access control (RBAC)
Geofencing Access depends on physical location
Exam tip

. RADIUS = network access (users). TACACS+ = device administration (admins) and encrypts the full payload. A self-signed certificate is not trusted by browsers.

3Physical security and deception

Item Meaning
Cameras, locks Detect and deter physical access (badges, rack locks, mantraps)
Honeypot A decoy system that attracts attackers so you can study and detect them
Honeynet A decoy network of honeypots

4Compliance and segmentation

Item Meaning
Data locality Where data is stored must follow legal rules
PCI DSS Payment card data security standard
GDPR EU personal data privacy regulation
Network segmentation enforcement Separate devices by risk with VLANs, firewalls and ACLs: IoT and IIoT devices, SCADA/ICS/OT systems (industrial control, keep isolated), guest, BYOD
Exam tip

. IoT, industrial control and guest devices belong in their own segments, away from sensitive systems.

Exam tip

. RADIUS authenticates network access; TACACS+ administers devices and encrypts the full payload.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Network administrators must be authenticated and authorized per command on switches, with the full payload encrypted. Which protocol fits?

  • ARADIUS
  • BLDAP
  • CTACACS+
  • DSAML
Show the answer

Answer: C. TACACS+ is used for device administration and encrypts the whole payload.

S2Wireless users must authenticate through 802.1X against a central server. Which protocol is typically used?

  • ARADIUS
  • BTACACS+
  • CTFTP
  • DSNMP
Show the answer

Answer: A. RADIUS provides network access authentication.

S3An unpatched web server is exposed to the internet. What does the unpatched flaw represent?

  • AA threat
  • BA vulnerability
  • CAn exploit
  • DA baseline
Show the answer

Answer: B. A weakness is a vulnerability; the attacker's code is the exploit.

S4A security team deploys a decoy server to learn how attackers behave. What is it?

  • AA screened subnet
  • BA jump box
  • CA honeypot
  • DA proxy
Show the answer

Answer: C. Honeypots are decoys to attract and study attackers.

S5A factory's industrial control systems must be protected from the corporate and guest networks. What should be implemented?

  • AA single flat network with strong passwords
  • BA wireless mesh network
  • CA faster uplink
  • DNetwork segmentation with strict firewall rules
Show the answer

Answer: D. Segmentation isolates OT and ICS systems.

S6Which certificate type is not trusted by browsers by default?

  • AA self-signed certificate
  • BA certificate signed by a public certificate authority
  • CA certificate issued by a trusted root
  • DA wildcard certificate from a public authority
Show the answer

Answer: A. Self-signed certificates have no trusted issuer.

5.2 Recall questions

R1What does the CIA triad stand for?

Show the answer

Confidentiality, integrity and availability.

R2What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?

Show the answer

A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit uses it.

R3Which protocol encrypts the entire payload, RADIUS or TACACS+?

Show the answer

TACACS+.

R4What is a honeynet?

Show the answer

A decoy network of honeypots.

R5What does SAML provide?

Show the answer

Federated web single sign-on.

R6Which regulation covers payment card data?

Show the answer

PCI DSS.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Terms CIA; threat, vulnerability, exploit, risk
AAA tools RADIUS (network access, UDP), TACACS+ (device admin, TCP, full encryption), LDAP, SAML, MFA, SSO
Authorization least privilege, RBAC, geofencing, time-based
Other PKI and self-signed, honeypot and honeynet, PCI DSS, GDPR, data locality, segmentation of IoT, OT, guest, BYOD
